easy.heading: Starting the Day with a Smile
easy.body:
Hey friends! I hope you have your coffee ready because today's easy puzzle was a lovely way to wake up. I started by looking at the single-cell constraints first. Cell 0,3 had a sum target of 5, and cell 1,0 needed a 6. These are basically freebies! Looking at my domino pile, the 5,2 and 3,6 were looking right at me. I put the 5 part of the 5,2 into that 0,3 spot and used the 6 from the 3,6 domino for the 1,0 spot.

Then I turned my attention to the big sum at the bottom. The region at 3,0, 3,1, and 3,2 needed to add up to 14. That is a pretty big number for just three spots. I realized I needed my big doubles here. The 5,5 and 4,4 dominoes were key. By placing the 3,2 and 3,3 domino carefully, I was able to fit the 5s and 4s where they belonged to hit that target of 14.

The equals region across the top row from 0,0 to 0,2 was the final piece of the puzzle. Once I had the other numbers in place, I saw that I needed three 2s to make that work. The 2,2 domino and the other half of my 5,2 domino fit perfectly. It is so satisfying when the last few pieces just click into place like that!

medium.heading: Finding the Flow in the Middle
medium.body:
This medium one had me thinking for an extra minute! The trickiest part was definitely the equals regions that zig-zagged across the middle. I started with the easiest targets first. Cell 2,0 had to be a 0, and cell 3,4 had to be a 1. Knowing those values immediately narrowed down which dominoes could go in those spots. I used the 5,0 and 0,1 dominoes to fill those gaps right away.

The region for cells 2,3, 3,1, 3,2, and 3,3 all had to be equal. That is a lot of cells for one number! I looked at my remaining dominoes and saw the 3,3 double. If I used those 3s in the bottom right, it would set the value for that whole region to 3. This meant cell 2,3 also had to be a 3. Working backward from there, I filled in the 1,3 and 2,6 dominoes.

The equals region at 0,2, 1,2, and 1,3 ended up needing 1s. It was like a little dance of numbers where one move forced the next. I almost tripped up on the 1,4 and 2,4 equals constraint, but the 5,3 domino saved the day. It really helps to keep an eye on which dominoes you have left in your tray so you do not try to use the same number twice!

hard.heading: A Real Brain Teaser to Finish
hard.body:
Wow, Rodolfo Kurchan really brought his game today! This hard puzzle had so many equals and sum constraints that it felt like a maze. My breakthrough came from the bottom corner. Cell 6,0 had a sum target of 0, which is always a great starting point because it has to be a zero. That meant the domino at 6,0 and 6,1 had to be the 6,0 one, since 6,1 was part of an equals chain.

The chain at 6,1, 6,2, and 6,3 all had to be the same number. Since the 6,0 domino put a 6 in cell 6,1, that meant the whole row needed to be 6s. Wait, I had to double check that! Looking at the dominoes, I used the 6,5 and 6,6 dominoes to fill that row. Once those were set, I could work on the sum of 6 in the 4,4, 5,4, 6,4 column. Since 6,4 ended up being a 0 from the 2,0 domino, I needed the other two cells to add up to 6.

The middle of the board was the toughest part. I had a less than 3 constraint at 2,2 and a greater than 3 constraint at 4,2. Balancing the 1,3, 2,1, and 4,2 dominoes around those rules took a few tries. I actually had to erase my first attempt! But once I realized the 6,6 domino had to go in a specific spot to help satisfy the equals region, everything else fell into line. This one definitely required a second cup of coffee!

explanation.tips: Focus on the single-cell targets first since they give you a guaranteed number to work around. Next, look for large equals regions because they limit your choices to only a few possible domino values. Finally, check your remaining dominoes frequently because often there is only one domino left in your pile that can actually fit a specific sum or target!
explanation.learned:
I learned that zero is your best friend in these puzzles. Whenever you see a sum target of zero or a very low number, it is a huge clue that limits which dominoes can even be considered for that spot. It really simplifies the grid quickly. 

I also noticed how important the doubles are. Today, the 5,5 and 6,6 dominoes were basically the anchors for the hardest parts of the grids. If you can figure out where a double goes, the rest of the area usually solves itself because you are placing two of the same number at once.

faqs.question: How do you solve the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: To solve Pips, you must place the given set of dominoes into the grid so that every cell follows the rules. Look for sum targets, equals signs, and comparison symbols like greater than or less than to figure out which numbers go where.

faqs.question: What does the equals sign mean in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: When multiple cells are connected in a region with an equals sign, it means every single cell in that group must contain the exact same number of pips.

faqs.question: Is there a trick to the sum targets in Pips?
faqs.answer: Yes! Always start with very small sums like 0 or 1, or very large sums. These have fewer possible combinations of dominoes, making them much easier to solve than middle-range numbers.

faqs.question: Can you use the same domino twice in one Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: No, you must use each domino from the provided list exactly once. If you find yourself needing a domino you have already placed, you know you have made a mistake somewhere else.

faqs.question: What do I do if I get stuck on a Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Try looking for empty regions that do not have a constraint. Often, the numbers in those cells are forced by the dominoes around them. You can also try working backwards from the dominoes you have left.
